title: Here Today, Gone Tomorrow – The Mirage of Prosperity in the 21st Century (The Henry George Foundation, Empirical Insights, 10 September 2026)
what_was_fetched: Full page fetched directly via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200, no paywall). Parsed to clean text; the complete article body and reader comments were read in full. Full-text fetch, no partial or secondary source.
verdict: ENRICH places/united-kingdom — update the page's ONS land-share figure to the newer 2024 vintage this essay cites, and add the essay's capitalisation argument as a short new passage (with a secondary cross-link candidate at concepts/economic-rent.md, which currently has no 'land value is a capitalised claim, not produced wealth' passage at all).
claim_grade: B — Henry George Foundation is a Tier-2 advocacy body under §4c (same as the essay already cited on places/united-kingdom.md), so it may be cited as an origin/proponent of the framing, never as independent proof; but its headline figures are each attributed by name to Tier-1 sources (ONS national balance-sheet data; the IFS Deaton Review of Inequalities) rather than asserted on the Foundation's own authority. Those attributions were not independently checked against the underlying ONS/IFS publications in this session, so treat as traceable-but-unverified pending a T1 pull of the primary releases.
content_summary: Argues Britain's headline wealth growth is misleading because land value is 'a capitalised claim on future economic surplus, not a produced contribution to national wealth' — quoted verbatim: 'Rising land values redistribute purchasing power but do not increase national wealth,' illustrated with a poker-chips-at-a-table analogy (one player's gain is another's loss; the total does not grow). Specific figures, each attributed to a named source: (1) IFS — housing was 11% of the wealth of the UK's top 1% and 22% of the top 10% in 1971, rising to 32% and 45% respectively by 2012 (citing Bourquin, Brewer & Wernham 2022, IFS Deaton Review of Inequalities); (2) IFS — pension wealth's share of household wealth rose 9 percentage points, from 38% to 47%, between 2006-08 and 2016-18, driven partly by falling annuity/discount rates rather than real income gains; (3) ONS — for April 2020–March 2022, net property wealth was still the largest household-wealth component at 40%, versus 35% for private pensions; (4) ONS — in 2024, 'non-produced assets' (the ONS's own definition of land) were 'almost 55%' of the UK's total net worth of £13.1 trillion, up from 'just under 40%' in 1995.
existing_wiki_coverage: places/united-kingdom.md already cites ONS for an earlier vintage of the same statistic — £6.3 trillion of land value out of £10.7 trillion net worth ('nearly three-fifths'), sourced to the ONS's March 2022 'Beneath our feet' blog post. This essay's 2024 figure (£13.1 trillion net worth, land ≈ 55%) is a materially different, more recent number that a T1 should reconcile against the actual ONS national balance-sheet release before folding into the page — note the land *share* appears to have fallen slightly (59%→55%) even as both totals rose, which is worth understanding rather than silently overwriting. The IFS wealth-composition-by-decile figures (1971 vs. 2012) and the pension-wealth-share figures (2006-08 vs. 2016-18) are not currently on any wiki page found in the corpus digest and would be new. The capitalisation/zero-sum argument itself — land value as a claim on future surplus rather than produced wealth — is not currently stated anywhere on concepts/economic-rent.md, which is otherwise the wiki's most-linked concept page (215 backlinks) and a natural home for it, properly attributed as the Foundation's argument rather than presented as settled fact.
uncertainties: 1. The 2024 ONS '55% of £13.1tn' figure was not independently verified against an ONS primary release in this session — only the essay's own attribution was read. 2. It is unclear whether the 2022-vintage figure already on places/united-kingdom.md and this 2024-vintage figure use the same ONS methodology/definition of 'non-produced assets,' so a T1 should not treat them as a simple time series without checking. 3. The essay is explicitly the first of a promised series ('Subsequent Empirical Insights articles will explore...'); later instalments may supersede or complicate this one and are not yet in the queue.

title: NYC's High-Value Property Tax: An In-Depth Look At The Pied-à-Terre Levy And Its Challenges (Dani R. Goldberg, Joshua Headley & Philip R. Hirschfeld, Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney PC, Mondaq, 7 September 2026)
what_was_fetched: Full page fetched directly via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200, no paywall, no bot-wall). Parsed to clean text; the complete article — body, both worked examples, exemptions section, entity-look-through rule, litigation history, and 'Trends Across the Nation' closer — was read in full. Full-text fetch, no partial or secondary source.
verdict: ENRICH places/new-york-city — genuine gap. No pied-à-terre or high-value-property surcharge content exists anywhere in the corpus digest or on the current places/new-york-city.md page; this is a real, currently-in-effect NYC tax with none of its specifics on the wiki.
claim_grade: B — law-firm client-alert content (Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney), Tier 2 under §4c for any opinion/framing, but treated per the Denmark Legal 500 precedent already on places/denmark.md as generally reliable on statutory facts, rates, thresholds and dates in the ordinary course of client-alert practice. Not independently checked here against the primary NYC Administrative Code / enabling state statute text, and no bill or local-law number is given anywhere in the article itself — a gap a T1 should close before publishing specifics.
content_summary: New York City's pied-à-terre tax on high-value non-primary residences took effect 1 July 2026, administered by the NYC Department of Finance, structured as an annual surcharge (not a transfer tax) in two valuation phases. Phase 1 (current, DOF-assessed values): Class One (1–3-family) homes taxed at 0.8% ($5M–$15M), 1.05% ($15,000,001–$25M), 1.3% (>$25M); condos/co-ops at 4.0% ($1M–$3M), 5.25% ($3,000,001–$5M), 6.5% (>$5M) — deliberately higher than Class One rates because co-op/condo assessments use an income-based method that understates market value. Phase 2 (from July 2028, comparable-sales valuation): Class One rates unchanged; condo/co-op brackets and rates drop to match Class One ($5M–$15M at 0.8%, etc.). Worked example: a $2M co-op valued by rental income owes ~$80,000/year (4% × $2M) in Phase 1; the same unit at $6M under comparable sales owes ~$48,000/year (0.8% × $6M) in Phase 2. Co-ops pay the surcharge corporately and charge it back to shareholders; unpaid amounts can lien the whole building. Exemptions: primary residences, family-occupied units, and units under a bona fide arm's-length lease of ≥ 1 year to an occupying tenant, with statutory look-through rules for trusts/LLCs/corporations (majority natural-person beneficiary/owner using it as a primary residence). Litigation: an 10 August 2026 state-court TRO barred DOF from imposing/collecting the tax over inadequate notice to homeowners; lifted 13 August 2026 after a Brooklyn Appellate Division ruling let the rollout continue pending further proceedings; exemption-filing deadline extended to 6 October 2026; the tax sunsets 30 June 2031 unless renewed. Quoted: 'the tax has already faced significant challenges.' The article's closing line groups NYC with 'Rhode Island, Hawaii and Montana' as states/cities that 'have implemented similar taxes on properties that are not primary residences' — directly relevant context for item 3 below.
existing_wiki_coverage: places/new-york-city.md currently covers Albouy et al./Barr-Smith-Kulkarni land-value estimates, the 1886 Henry George mayoral campaign, the 1921–1931 building-tax exemption, the 2025 congestion-pricing study, and the 2026 Section 119-r transit value-capture renewal — nothing on residential property-tax surcharges or the pied-à-terre levy specifically. people/lawson-purdy.md (NYC's historical land/building assessment split) is thematically adjacent but does not cover this. No other wiki page (concepts/split-rate-taxation.md, concepts/mansion-tax equivalents) was found to duplicate this content.
uncertainties: 1. No local-law or state-enabling-statute citation is given in the article — NYC generally needs Albany authorization for new property levies, so a T1 should confirm whether this rests on a specific state enabling act before treating it as purely city-originated. 2. The current litigation status beyond 13 August 2026 (whether further TROs, appeals, or a final ruling followed before this brief's 21 September 2026 date) was not checked against any other source — only this article's own account, current as of its 7 September 2026 publication date, was read. 3. The article's claim that Rhode Island, Hawaii and Montana have 'similar taxes' was not independently verified for Rhode Island or Hawaii in this session (Montana's 2026 second-home/short-term-rental rate, covered in item 3 below, is a genuine parallel but is a classification-rate system, not a transfer or surcharge tax of NYC's design — the comparison in the source article is looser than the wiki should be).

title: 2026 Tax Information for Montana Property Owners (Montana Department of Revenue, revenue.mt.gov)
what_was_fetched: Full page fetched directly via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200, no paywall, no bot-wall, no JS-dependent content). Parsed to clean text; the entire page — every rate table (primary residence/long-term rental, second home/short-term rental, multifamily, manufactured homes, commercial/industrial, non-qualified and qualified agricultural land, forest land) — was read in full. This is the wiki queue's designated canonical primary source; no secondary corroboration was sought or needed for the rate figures themselves, which are a direct official statement.
verdict: DEFER — do not create places/montana.md from this source alone. Recommend queuing a follow-up search for the enacting 2025-session Montana legislative bill (the page's reference to a '2025 property tax rebate' implies a predecessor reform) before building a page; in the meantime this source could support a short, precisely-worded addition, but no natural existing page fits well (see below) so the safer call is to hold it rather than force a weak fit.
claim_grade: A — official primary source (Montana Department of Revenue), directly stating the state's own current-year tax rates with no interpretation required. The one caveat: the page cites no bill or session-law number for the reform itself, so the precise legislative provenance is unverified from this document alone.
content_summary: PRECISE CLASSIFICATION (per the task's caution about classification confusion): this is NOT a land value tax and NOT a split-rate (land-vs-improvement) tax. It is a use-classification / homestead-style rate schedule applied to each property's total market value (land and improvements together, not separated), 2026 tax year. Primary residences and long-term rentals (rented ≥28 days for ≥7 months/year; application window 1 Dec 2025–1 Mar 2026; automatic requalification for 2025 property-tax-rebate recipients who still occupy) get a tiered/marginal-bracket rate: 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value, 0.90% on $378,001–$756,000, 1.10% on $756,001–$1,511,999, 1.90% on the portion above $1,512,000. Second homes, short-term rentals (VRBO/Airbnb/cabins) and vacant residential lots instead pay a flat 1.90% on the ENTIRE value from dollar one — i.e., the reform is functionally a primary-residence/long-term-rental discount layered onto an otherwise-flat top rate, not a land-value mechanism. Multifamily long-term-rental buildings: flat 1.10%. Manufactured/mobile homes get the tiered rate if used as primary residence/long-term rental (with up to 1 acre of co-owned land included). Commercial/industrial property: two-tier flat structure, 1.50% below 6× the estimated statewide median value ($379,000, i.e., below $2,274,000) and 1.90% at or above it. Non-qualified agricultural land: flat 14.35% on the land itself, with any home + 1-acre homesite taxed separately at the tiered residential rate (if primary/long-term rental) or flat 1.90% (if second home/short-term rental). Qualified agricultural land (auto-qualifies at 160+ acres, else requires proof of agricultural use/income): flat 2.05% on land, with the residence taxed at the tiered rate (primary/long-term) or a flat 1.35% (second home/short-term rental) — notably lower than the non-agricultural second-home rate. Forest land: flat 0.37% on land, with the dwelling taxed at the tiered rate (primary) or flat 1.90% (second home/short-term).
existing_wiki_coverage: The wiki's only existing Montana content is research/gaffney-montana-land-policy.md, Mason Gaffney's 1977 'Counter-colonial Land Policy for Montana' address — which argues Montana is an internal resource colony (absentee-owned coal/minerals, mercantilist rail rates, extractive-industry tax favoritism) and prescribes land value taxation. That page's subject matter (resource-rent/severance-tax policy, coal, absentee ownership) is thematically distant from this 2026 residential/agricultural property-tax classification reform; grafting a note about 2026 rates onto it would be a forced fit unless done very briefly as a 'current context' aside. There is no places/montana.md and no concepts/homestead-exemption.md anywhere in the corpus — both are genuine gaps, but this single DOR rates page cannot carry either alone (see verdict).
uncertainties: 1. The enacting legislation is not named on this page — the reference to a '2025 property tax rebate' as an automatic-qualification pathway implies a predecessor 2025-session reform (plausibly Montana's widely-reported property-tax/reappraisal relief package), but the specific bill/session-law number was not found or verified here and would be needed for any new page's legislative-history section. 2. Whether this reform followed, or was a response to, Montana's high-profile 2023 reappraisal-driven tax-bill spike (a matter of some public controversy in the state) is plausible context but was not confirmed from this source. 3. A proper places/montana.md would need distributional evidence (who actually gains/loses — presumably primary/long-term-rental owners versus second-home, short-term-rental and out-of-state owners) and at least one independent (journalistic or academic) assessment of the reform's effects, neither of which this official rates page supplies. 4. Whether any Montana locality separately runs or has proposed an actual land-value or split-rate system (which would be the genuinely on-mission finding) was not investigated in this session and remains open.
